scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

message.reasoning: The scenario describes a conflict between parents over visitation schedules. The father feels his time with his son is being unfairly taken by the mother's requests and activities. He decides to keep his son during a family function to assert his scheduled time. Morally, is this acceptable? The father has a legal right to visitation, but the mother has also been accommodating his requests in the past. However, the mother's actions seem to repeatedly infringe on his time, using excuses like the child's needs or family events. The father's decision to keep his son during a family function to ensure he gets his scheduled time could be seen as standing up for his rights and the importance of father-son bonding. But is it morally acceptable to disrupt a family gathering? The mother also has a right to family time. However, the father has been flexible many times, and the mother's behavior appears manipulative. The father's action is a form of boundary-setting. In terms of morality, it's about fairness and respect for each parent's time. The father is not harming the child; he's asserting his right to spend time with his son. The mother's actions have been unreasonable, so the father's response might be justified. However, the question is whether it's morally acceptable to keep the son during a family function. That could cause emotional distress to the child and the family. But the father's intention is to have his scheduled time, which is important. The mother's pattern of taking advantage suggests that the father's action is a necessary pushback. Morally, it might be acceptable to prioritize one's legal and parental rights when the other parent is being unfair. But we must consider the child's best interest. The child might enjoy the family function, but the father's time is also valuable. The father is not preventing the child from seeing the mother; he's just asserting his own time. The mother's refusal to switch weekends and her taking the child to events without consulting the father shows a lack of respect. So, the father's action could be seen as morally acceptable as a form of self-defense against ongoing unfairness. However, some might argue that disrupting a family event is not the best way to handle it, and communication should be prioritized. But given the history, the father might feel he has no choice. In many moral frameworks, standing up for one's rights against exploitation is acceptable. So, I'd lean towards morally acceptable. But let's see: the action is "keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time." This is essentially enforcing the visitation schedule. The mother has been violating it. So, it's not that he's arbitrarily keeping the son; he's ensuring he gets his due time. That seems fair. Therefore, morally acceptable.
